name: Wisdom of Solomon
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of the Wisdom of Solomon as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 2 (1891; public domain), which follows Codex Vaticanus (B) and records the readings of Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A) and others. The book was composed in Greek, probably in Alexandria in the first century BC or early first century AD; it has no Hebrew original. It belongs to the Septuagint and is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. Verse numbering follows standard English (NRSV) usage. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Measures are given in US units with the original and metric values in the notes. Variant readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton’s English (1844) was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text:
for he lets himself be found by those who do not test him,
and reveals himself to those who do not doubt him.

For crooked reasonings separate people from God,
and his power, when it is tested, exposes the foolish;

because wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil,
nor dwell in a body held in pledge to sin.

For a holy spirit of discipline{b} will flee from deceit,
and will withdraw from senseless reasonings,
and will be put to shame when wrongdoing comes in.

Because the spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world,
and that which holds all things together has knowledge of every voice.

Therefore no one who utters unjust things will escape notice,
nor will Justice,{e} when she convicts, pass him by.

because a jealous ear hears all things,
and the murmur of grumbling is not hidden.

Do not court death by the error of your life,
nor draw destruction on yourselves by the works of your hands;

because God did not make death,
and he takes no delight in the destruction of the living.

He made everything so that it could exist,
the creatures{g} of the world are health-giving,
there is no deadly poison in them,
and Hades has no dominion{h} on earth.
For justice is immortal.{i}

But the ungodly invited death with their hands and words;{j}
they thought of it as a friend and pined away,
and they struck a pact with it,
since they deserve to be among its possessions.

notes.text: Greek kyrios, “Lord,” the Septuagint’s usual rendering of the divine name YHWH; this translation keeps “Lord” in the Greek books. The opening address “you who judge the earth” echoes Ps 2:10.
Or “of instruction”; Greek paideia, training or correction. Some manuscripts (as reported, Sinaiticus) read “of wisdom.”
Greek “his kidneys,” thought of as the seat of the emotions.
Greek dikē, justice personified as an avenging power.
Or “goes unpunished”; Greek “will not go empty.”
Or “the creatures,” “the things that come into being”; Greek geneseis.
The Latin tradition adds a further line, “but injustice is the acquisition of death,” which is not in the Greek manuscripts used here.

verses.text:
For, reckoning wrongly, they said to themselves,
“Brief and full of grief is this life of ours,
and for a mortal’s end there is no cure,
nor is anyone known who has come back{a} out of Hades.

when it is put out, the body will turn to ashes,
and the spirit will be scattered like thin air.

In time our name will be forgotten,
and nobody will recall what we did;
our lives will vanish like the remnants of a cloud,
and disperse like fog
driven off by the sun’s beams
and pressed down by its warmth.

For our allotted time is the passing of a shadow,
and there is no going back from our end,
because it is sealed up and no one turns it back.

“Come, then, let us enjoy the good things that are present,
and make use of the creation{b} eagerly, as in youth.

With wine of great price and with perfumes let us be filled,
and let no blossom of spring{c} get by us.
Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they wither.

But let our strength be our law of justice,
for what is weak proves itself useless.

“Let us lie in wait for the just man, because he is inconvenient to us,
and he opposes our deeds;
he reproaches us for sins against the law,
and charges us with sins against our training.

He claims to possess knowledge of God,
and names himself a son{d} of the Lord.

He has become to us a reproof of our thoughts;
he is a burden to us even to look at,

because his life is unlike that of others,
and his paths are of another kind.

We are counted by him as something counterfeit,
and he keeps away from our ways as from uncleanness;
he calls the last end of the just happy,
and boasts that God is his father.

Let us find out whether what he says is true,
and make trial of how things go with him when he departs.

For if the just man is God’s son, he will help him,
and will rescue him from the hand of his adversaries.

Let us examine him with insult and torture,
so that we may know his gentleness,
and put his forbearance to the proof.

Let us condemn him to a shameful death,
for, according to his words, he will be watched over.”{e}

Thus they reasoned, and they were led astray,
for their wickedness blinded them,

for God created humankind for incorruption,
and made it the image of his own eternity;{g}

but death entered the world through the devil’s{h} jealousy,
and those on his side experience it.

notes.text: Some manuscripts read “flower of the air”; others “flower of life.”
Or “servant”; Greek pais can mean either.
Literally “for there will be a visitation of him according to his words.”
Some manuscripts read “of his own nature” (Greek idiotētos for aidiotētos), as reported.
Greek diabolos, “slanderer,” here commonly understood of the serpent of Gen 3.

verses.text:
But the souls of the just are in the hand of God,
and no torment will ever{a} touch them.

In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died,
and their departure was reckoned an affliction,

and their going from us a ruin;
but they are at peace.

For though in the sight of people they were punished,
their hope is full of immortality.

After a small correction they will receive great blessings,
for God tried them and judged them fit for himself;

like gold in the furnace he tried them,
and like a whole burnt offering{b} he accepted them.

In the time of their visitation they will shine out,
and they will run like sparks through stubble.

Nations they shall judge, over peoples they shall hold sway,
and over them the Lord shall be king to the ages.

But the ungodly will receive punishment as their reasonings deserve,
those who disregarded the just{d} and rebelled against the Lord;

Their wives are foolish, and their children evil;
cursed is their offspring.

Blessed too the eunuch who has worked no lawless thing with his hand
nor plotted evil things against the Lord;
to him a chosen gift shall be given for his fidelity,
and in the Lord’s sanctuary a portion all the more delightful.

For good toil yields a fruit of glory,
and the root of good sense never gives way.

But the children of adulterers will never mature,
and the offspring of an illicit union will disappear.

Even if they live long, they will be counted as nothing,
and at the last their old age will be without honor.

Should they die quickly, hope is not theirs,
nor any comfort in the day when the verdict is given.{e}
For hard is the end of an unrighteous generation.

notes.text: The Greek uses an emphatic double negative.
Greek holokarpōma, a sacrifice wholly consumed on the altar.
Some manuscripts add “and he watches over his holy ones,” as at 4:15.
Greek “of decision,” that is, of the verdict.

verses.text:
Though for a season they may sprout in branches,
yet, set unsteadily, they will be rocked by the wind
and torn up by the roots under the gales’ force.

Their shoots will be snapped off unfinished,
their fruit worthless,
unripe for food, fit for nothing at all.

For children born of unlawful unions{b}
are witnesses of wickedness against their parents when they are examined.
But the just, though he come to his end early, will be at rest.

For honorable old age is not that of long time,
nor is it measured by number of years;

but understanding is gray hair for human beings,
and a spotless life is ripe old age.

Being pleasing to God, he was loved,
and while living among sinners he was taken up.{c}

He was snatched away so that evil might not alter his understanding
or guile deceive his soul.

For the bewitching of trivial things obscures what is good,
and the roving of desire perverts an innocent mind.
Made complete in a brief span, he filled out lengthy times;

for his soul was pleasing to the Lord;
therefore he hurried him{d} out of the midst of wickedness.
But the peoples saw and did not understand,
nor did they take such a thing to heart,

that grace and mercy are with his chosen ones,
and he watches over his holy ones.

A righteous person who has died will judge the living ungodly,
and a youth swiftly made complete will judge the long old age of the unrighteous.

They will look on the wise man’s death
without grasping what the Lord intended for him
or why he set him in safety.

They will look on and sneer,
but the Lord will mock them.

Cowering, they will come to the counting of their sins,
and their own lawless acts will stand opposite and accuse them.

notes.text: Greek metetethē, the word used of Enoch in Gen 5:24 (Septuagint).
Or “it hurried”; the subject may be the soul.

verses.text:
Then the righteous one will take his stand with much boldness
facing those who afflicted him
and who set his toils at nothing.

At the sight they will be thrown into turmoil by a terrible fear
and stand astonished at a deliverance beyond all expectation.

Repenting, they will say to one another,
and groan through distress of spirit:

“This is the man we used to laugh at,
whom we made a proverb of scorn — senseless that we were!
His way of life we counted lunacy,
and his death a dishonor.

How has he been numbered among the children{a} of God,
and his lot is among the holy ones?

What did our arrogance profit us?
And what good has wealth, with our boasting, brought us?

“All those things have passed away like a shadow,
and like a rumor that runs by;

or as with a bird darting through the air:
no mark of its course is to be found,
but the slight breeze, whipped by the stroke of its feathers
and split by its whirring force,
is crossed by its beating wings,
and afterward nothing in it shows that it went that way;

or as, when an arrow is shot at a target,
the air, cut through, at once closes up again,
so that no one knows its pathway.

So it is with us: no sooner were we born than we ceased to exist,
and we had no mark of virtue to display,
but were used up in our wickedness.”

For the hope of the ungodly is like chaff{b} carried by the wind,
and like fine frost{c} driven away by a storm;
it is scattered like smoke before the wind,
and it passes like the memory of a guest who stays a single day.

But the righteous live to the age,
in the Lord is their recompense,
and the Most High takes thought for them.

Therefore they will receive a majestic kingdom
and a beautiful crown from the Lord’s hand,
for he will cover them with his right hand
and protect them with his arm.

He will take his zeal as his full armor,
and will arm creation to repel his enemies;

he will put on justice as a breastplate,
and wear impartial judgment as a helmet;
he will take holiness as an invincible shield,

he will whet unbending anger into a blade,
and the world{d} will go to war at his side against those who have lost their senses.

Well-aimed shafts of lightning will fly,
and as from a well-drawn bow of clouds they will leap to the target,

a blast of might{e} will stand up against them
and scatter them like a whirlwind winnowing grain.
So lawlessness will turn the whole earth to desert,
and ill-doing will topple the seats of the powerful.

notes.text: Greek “sons”; the “holy ones” may be angels.
Greek chnous, fine down or dust.
Some manuscripts read “spider’s web” (Greek arachnē for pachnē), as reported.

verses.text:
Listen, therefore, you kings, and understand;
learn, you judges of the ends of the earth.

Give ear, you who rule over multitudes,
and who take pride in throngs of nations.

For your authority came to you from the Lord,
and your rule from the Most High,
who will examine what you do and scrutinize your plans.

For though you were ministers of his reign, you gave no upright judgment,
you did not guard the law,
and you did not walk by God’s design.

Fearfully and fast he will stand over you,
since on those who stand high a sharp judgment comes.

The least may be forgiven out of pity,
but the strong will be strongly examined.

For the Master of all does not back away before anyone,
and is not impressed by rank,
since he made small and great alike,
and cares for them all equally.
For the mighty a stern scrutiny lies ahead.

To you, then, O sovereigns, my words are addressed,
so that you may learn wisdom and not fall away.

For those who keep holy things in holiness will be made holy,
and those who have been taught them will find a defense.

Therefore set your desire on my words;
long for them, and you will be instructed.

Wisdom is bright and never fades,
readily noticed by those who love her,
and discovered by those who look for her.
She is quick to be recognized by those who long for her, coming to meet them first.

Whoever rises early to seek her will not grow weary,
for he will find her sitting at his gates.

To think upon her is the perfection of understanding,
and whoever keeps vigil for her sake will soon be free from care,

Her starting point is the truest longing for discipline;
and care for discipline is love;

and love of her is the keeping of her laws,
and attention to her laws is assurance of incorruption,
and incorruption brings one near to God;
Thus the longing for wisdom raises one up to royal rule.{a}

If, then, you delight in thrones and scepters, O sovereigns of peoples,
honor wisdom, so that you may reign for ever.

What wisdom is and how she came to be I will declare,
and I will not hide secret things from you,
but I will trace her out from the beginning of creation,
and bring the knowledge of her into the open,
and I will not pass by the truth;

nor will I travel in company with wasting envy,
for envy has no fellowship with wisdom.

A host of the wise keeps the world safe,
and a prudent king is the steadiness of a people.
Therefore be instructed by my words, and you will profit.

notes.text: Verses 17–20 form a chain argument (sorites), each clause taking up the last word of the one before.

verses.text:
within a period of ten months,{b} curdled in blood
from a man’s seed and the pleasure that comes with sleep.
I was nursed in swaddling clothes and with cares.
For no king has had any other beginning of existence;
there is for all one entrance into life, and a like departure.

Therefore I prayed, and understanding was granted me;
I called upon God, and a spirit of wisdom came to me.

I preferred her before scepters and thrones,
and wealth I held as nothing beside her.

Beyond health and good looks I loved her,
and I chose to have her rather than light,
because the radiance that comes from her never sleeps.

Together with her all good things came to me,
and in her hands wealth past counting.

Over all of them I was glad, since wisdom goes at their head,
though I was unaware that she was the one who bore{c} them.

Without guile I learned, and without grudging I share;
I do not hide away her riches;

For in his hand are both we ourselves and our sayings,
and all good sense and the know-how of the crafts.

He himself gave me true knowledge of the things that are:
to know how the universe is put together and how its elements act;

the beginning and end and middle of times,
the shifts of the solstices{e} and the changes of the seasons,
the cycles of years and the positions of the stars,

whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest I learned,
for wisdom, the artisan of all things, taught me.

For there is in her a spirit, thinking and holy,
only-begotten, many-sided, fine,
quick to move, distinct, unsoiled,
plain, unharmed, fond of the good, sharp,

unhindered, beneficent, humane,
steadfast, sure, free from care,
all-powerful, overseeing all,
and passing through all spirits
that are intelligent, pure, and most subtle.{g}

For wisdom is more mobile than any motion;
because of her purity she pervades and penetrates all things.

For she is a reflected radiance of everlasting light,
a spotless mirror of the working of God,
and an image of his goodness.
For God loves nothing except the one who lives together with wisdom.

for night succeeds to it,
but against wisdom evil does not prevail.

notes.text: Ten lunar months, about nine calendar months.
Greek genesin, “origin” or “begetter”; some manuscripts read genetin, “mother.”
Greek tropōn, “turnings,” the turning points of the sun’s course.
Verses 22–23 list twenty-one attributes (3 × 7), a number of perfection.

verses.text:
From end to end she stretches out in strength,
and she manages the whole well.

She proclaims her noble birth by living with God,
and the Master of all loved her.

For she is an initiate in the knowledge of God,
and one who chooses among his works.

If riches are a possession to be desired in life,
what is richer than wisdom, who works all things?

And if understanding is at work,
who more than she is the artisan of what exists?

So I resolved to bring her home to live with me,
knowing she would advise me well
and comfort me in worry and sorrow.

Through her I will gain fame among crowds
and respect from the elders, young as I am.

Sharp I shall be found in giving judgment,
and before the powerful I shall be a marvel.

When I am quiet they will wait on me,
and when I speak they will pay attention,
and if I go on talking, they will put hands over their mouths.

Through her I shall possess deathlessness,
and I shall leave to those who come after me a memory that lasts for ever.

I shall order the affairs of peoples,
and nations shall be made subject to me.

Fearsome tyrants will be afraid when they hear of me;
I will prove kind toward the people, and brave in battle.

Turning these things over within myself,
and weighing them in my heart,
that deathlessness lies in being akin to wisdom,

and good delight in her friendship,
and in the toils of her hands riches that do not run out,
and good sense in practice at her side,
and fair fame in taking part in her words,
I went all around searching how I might take her for my own.

I was a child of good nature,
and a good soul fell to my lot;
or rather, being good, I entered an undefiled body.{b}

But perceiving that I would not otherwise gain possession of her unless God gave her —
and it was a mark of understanding to know whose gift she was —
I appealed to the Lord and implored him,
and with my whole heart I said:

notes.text: The four cardinal virtues of Greek philosophy.
The verse reflects the Greek idea of the soul’s existence before the body; verse 19 states it the other way.

verses.text:
“God of the fathers and Lord of mercy,
who made all things by your word,

and by your wisdom formed humankind
to have dominion over the creatures that came into being by you,

and to govern the world in holiness and justice,
and to pronounce judgment in uprightness of soul,

grant me the wisdom that shares the seat of your thrones,
and do not reject me from among your children.{a}

for even if one is perfect among the children of men,
yet without the wisdom that comes from you he will be counted as nothing.

It was you who picked me as king of your people
and as judge of your sons and your daughters.

You ordered me to build a sanctuary on your holy mountain,
and an altar in the city where you make your dwelling,
a replica of the sacred tent you prepared long ago.

Wisdom is with you; she knows what you do
and was there when you created the world,
she grasps what pleases you
and what accords with your commands.

Send her forth from the holy heavens,
and from the throne of your glory dispatch her,
that she may be with me and labor with me,
and that I may learn what is pleasing to you.

For she knows all things and has insight into them,
and in what I do she will lead me with good sense
and keep watch over me by her glory.

“For what human being can learn the counsel of God?
Or who can conceive what the Lord wills?

For the reasonings of mortals are timid,
and our designs are likely to fail;

for a perishable body weighs down the soul,
and this earthly tent burdens the mind that ponders many things.

Who has learned your counsel, unless you gave wisdom
and sent your holy spirit from on high?

So it was that the ways of earth’s dwellers were made straight,
and human beings learned the things that please you,
and through wisdom they were brought to safety.”

She it was who guarded the father of the world, the first to be shaped,
when he had been created alone,
and drew him out of his own fall,
and gave him strength to rule over all things.

But when one who was unjust{a} turned from her in his anger,
he was destroyed together with the brother-killing rage he gave way to.

And when because of him the earth was drowned, wisdom saved it once more,
piloting the righteous one{b} on a cheap timber.

She rescued a just man{e} when the ungodly were perishing;
he fled from the fire that came down on the Five Cities.

To their evil there still bears witness
a smoking land left waste,
and plants that bear fruit not brought to its time,
and, standing as a memorial of a soul without faith, a pillar of salt.

For they walked past wisdom
and so were not merely harmed by not knowing what is good,
but also left to the living a monument to their senselessness,
that what they stumbled in might not escape notice.
Wisdom rescued from troubles those who served her.

She guided a righteous one{f} along straight paths
when he fled from the anger of his brother;
she let him see God’s kingdom,
she gave him the knowledge of holy things,
she made him thrive in his hard work
and multiplied what his labors produced.

In the greed of those who overpowered him she stood at his side
and gave him wealth.

When a just man{h} was sold, she did not abandon him,
but rescued him from sin.

She descended with him into the pit,
and did not abandon him in his chains,
until she delivered to him a royal scepter
and power over those who had oppressed him;
she exposed his accusers as liars,
and granted him lasting glory.

A holy people and a blameless offspring
she delivered from a nation of oppressors.

Into the soul of the Lord’s attendant{i} she went,
and she stood up to fearsome kings with portents and signs.

To the holy ones she paid out the reward of their toil;
she led them on a wonderful road,
and she was for them a covering in the day
and a blaze of stars all night.

She brought them over the Red Sea,
and led them through deep waters;

but their enemies she drowned,
and cast them up from the depth of the abyss.

for wisdom opened the mouths of the mute,
and made the tongues of infants speak clearly.

notes.text: Cain (Gen 4). Throughout chapters 10–19 the biblical figures are not named.
Lot (Gen 19). The “Five Cities” (Greek Pentapolis) are those of Gen 14:2.

verses.text: She prospered their works by the hand of a holy prophet.

Through a desert where no one lived they made their way,
and in places with no path they set up their tents.
They took a stand against those at war with them and beat back their enemies.

They were thirsty and called on you,
and from a sheer cliff water was given them,
and from hard rock relief from thirst.

For by the very means through which their foes were chastised,
by these, when they were at a loss, they received benefit.{a}

In place of a river’s ever-running spring
churned with gore and filth{b}

as a reproof of the order to murder the babies,
you gave them plenty of water when they had no hope of it,

making plain by the thirst they then felt
in what manner you chastised their opponents.

For when they were put to the test, though they were being corrected with mercy,
they learned how the ungodly suffered when judged with anger.

For you tested them as a father does in warning,
but you examined the others as a stern king does in condemnation.
Whether absent or present, they were equally distressed,

for double sorrow gripped them,
and they moaned as they remembered the past.

For when they heard that through their own punishments
the others had been benefited, they perceived the Lord.

For the one whom long before they had cast out and exposed{c}
and then rejected with scorn,
him they admired at the end of the events,
having thirsted in a way unlike the just.
so they would know that the instruments of someone’s sin are the instruments of his punishment.

For your almighty hand,
which fashioned the world from shapeless matter,
had no shortage of ways to send a horde of bears or fierce lions against them,

or newly created unknown beasts full of rage,
either breathing out fiery breath,
or belching thick smoke,
or flashing terrible sparks from their eyes;

not only could their harm destroy them utterly,
but even the very sight of them could kill by fright.

Even without these, they could have been felled by one breath,
hunted down by justice
and blown away by your mighty spirit.
But you have ordered everything by measure, number, and weight.

For great might is ever at your side,
and the strength of your arm, who shall stand against it?

The whole universe before you is like the small weight that turns a balance,{e}
and like a dewdrop at dawn coming down to the ground.

But you are merciful to all, because you can do everything,
and you pass over human sins so that people may repent.

How would anything remain if you did not wish it?
Or what you had not called, how would it be kept?
You spare all things, because they are yours, O Master, lover of souls.{f}

notes.text: The theme of chapters 11–19: the same elements that punished Egypt benefited Israel.

verses.text: For your incorruptible spirit is in all things.

So those who slip you reprove bit by bit,
and in the things where they go wrong you remind and admonish them,
that they may be set free from evil and put their trust, Lord, in you.
For the ancient dwellers in your holy land{a}

you hated, because they practiced hateful deeds,
acts of witchcraft and impious rites,

and parents who slaughtered souls that had no helper,
you resolved to wipe out by our fathers’ hands,

so that the land most precious of all in your sight
might receive a worthy colony of God’s children.{c}

not that you could not hand the ungodly over to the righteous in a battle line,
or rub them out all together through terrible beasts or a harsh word;

But by judging them gradually you gave them time to repent,
though you knew well that their origin was wicked,
their evil was inborn,
and their thinking would never change.

For their seed was cursed from the start,{e}
nor was it out of fear of anyone that you granted impunity for what they did wrong.

For who shall say, “What did you do?”
Or who shall stand up against your sentence?
Who shall charge you over nations destroyed that you yourself had made?
Or who shall come and stand against you as pleader for unrighteous men?

There is no god but you, who cares for all,
that you should show him your verdicts were not unjust;

nor shall king or tyrant be able to look you in the face
on behalf of those you have punished.

Being righteous, you order all things righteously,
and you judge it foreign to your might
to pass sentence on one who ought not to be chastised.

For your strength is the source of justice,
and your sovereignty over all causes you to spare all.

For you display strength when someone doubts that your power is complete,
and among those who do know it you put boldness to shame.

By such deeds you taught your people
that the righteous man must be a lover of humankind,
and you made your sons to be of good hope,
that for sins you grant a change of mind.

For if the enemies of your children, who were owed death,
you punished with such heed and such pardon,
giving them times and room in which to be rid of evil,

with what exactness you have judged your own sons,
to whose fathers you gave oaths and covenants of good pledges!

So while you discipline us, you strike our enemies ten thousand times harder,
so that we think of your goodness when we judge,
and expect mercy when we ourselves are judged.

So those who lived unjustly and foolishly
you tormented with their own abominations.

For they wandered very far along the roads of going astray,
taking for gods the most worthless and dishonored of animals,
fooled the way infants are who have no sense.

And so, as on children without reason,
you sent a judgment that made sport of them.

But those not set right by playful rebukes of correction
shall find a judgment worthy of God.

For in the very things that made them suffer and chafe,
in the things they counted gods and by which they were punished,
they saw and acknowledged as true God him whom they had refused to know before;
and so the utmost sentence came down on them.

notes.text: The Greek of verses 5–6 is difficult and the text may be corrupt.
Compare the curse of Canaan, Gen 9:25.

verses.text:
but either fire or wind or swift air,
or the circle of the stars or rushing water
or the lights of heaven, governors of the world, they took for gods.

and if they were struck with wonder at their power and working,
let them perceive from these how much more powerful is the one who formed them.

For from the greatness and beauty of created things
their Maker is seen by analogy.{b}

for, living among his works, they search,
and they are won over by the sight, because what they see is beautiful.
But again, not even they are to be pardoned;

But wretched, with their hopes in dead things, are those
who called the works of human hands gods,
gold and silver, worked with skill, and likenesses of living things,
or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand.

Suppose a woodcutter saws down a tree easy to handle,
skillfully strips off all its bark,
and, shaping it handsomely,
makes a useful vessel for the service of life,

and burns the leftovers of his work
to cook his food and eat his fill;

and the leftover from these, good for nothing,
a crooked stick grown full of knots,
he takes and carves with the care of his idle hours,
and shapes it with the experience of his leisure;{d}
he forms it into the image of a man,

then, making for it a dwelling worthy of it,
he sets it in the wall and fastens it with iron.

So he takes thought for it that it may not fall,
knowing that it cannot help itself,
for it is an image and needs help.

and for getting and working and good fortune in the use of his hands
he begs strong handiness of the thing most helpless in its hands.

notes.text: Greek ton onta, “the one who is,” echoing the Septuagint of Exod 3:14.
Some manuscripts read “with the skill of understanding.” Compare Isa 44:9–20.

verses.text:
Again, someone preparing to sail and about to cross the wild waves
calls upon a piece of wood more rotten than the vessel that carries him.

For that boat was thought up by the craving for profit,
and wisdom as craftswoman put it together;

but it is your providence, Father, that steers it,
because you have given it a way even in the sea
and a safe path among the waves,

showing that you can save from every danger,
so that even one without skill may go aboard.
For blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes;{b}

but the handmade thing is accursed, both it and the one who made it —
he, because he worked it, and the perishable thing, because it was named a god.
For hated alike by God are the impious and his impiety;
For the deed done shall be chastised along with its doer.

So on the idols of the nations too there shall come a visitation,
since among the things God made they turned into a loathsome thing,
traps for human souls
and a noose for the feet of fools.

For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication,{c}
and their invention the corruption of life;

For they were not there at the start,
and they shall not remain to the age;

For through the empty conceit of human beings they entered the world,
and therefore a speedy end has been planned for them.

For a father, consumed with untimely grief
for a child suddenly taken from him,
made an image of him,
and now honored as a god one who was once a dead human being,
and handed on to those under him mysteries and initiations.

Then, strengthened by time, the impious habit was guarded as if it were law,
and by order of tyrants the carved figures received worship.

When people could not honor kings face to face, since they lived far away,
they imagined the king’s likeness from a distance
and made a visible statue of the king they revered,
so that in their eagerness they could flatter the absent king as if he were there.

And to heighten the cult even among those who did not know him,
the craftsman’s love of distinction pushed them on.

For he, wishing perhaps to gratify the man in power,
used his art to force the likeness into something finer;

and the crowd, drawn in by the charm of the workmanship,
now reckoned as an object of reverence the one they had a little earlier honored as a man.

Then it was not enough for them to go wrong about knowing God,
but living in a great war of ignorance,
they label such terrible evils peace.

For whether they practice child-slaying rites or secret mysteries,
or hold frenzied revels with strange laws,

and all is a confusion of blood and murder, theft and deceit,
corruption, faithlessness, tumult, perjury,

For worshiping idols that must not even be named{f}
is the start, source, and end of all evil.

For they either rave in their merriment, or prophesy lies,
or live unjustly, or readily commit perjury;

for since they trust in lifeless idols,
they swear wickedly and expect to suffer no harm.

But on both counts what is just will come after them:
that they thought badly of God, attaching themselves to idols,
and that they swore unjustly and with guile, holding holiness in contempt.

For it is not the power of what people swear by,
but the righteous penalty for sinners,
that always catches up with the wrongdoing of the unjust.

notes.text: Later Christian writers applied this line to the cross; in its setting it refers to the ark.
Here, as often in the prophets, a figure for unfaithfulness to God.
Greek geneseōs enallagē, “exchange of origin”; the sense is disputed, perhaps “perversion of nature.”

verses.text:
But you, our God, are kind and truthful,
long-suffering, governing everything with mercy.

For even if we sin, we are yours, aware of your might;
but we will not sin, knowing that you count us as yours.

For to be acquainted with you is righteousness made whole,
and to recognize your might is the taproot of deathlessness.

We have not been led astray by what human craft has wickedly devised,
nor by the barren toil of those who paint shadow-pictures,
a shape smeared with assorted colors,

the sight of which comes to fools as a reproach,{a}
and one longs for the breathless form of a dead likeness.

Lovers of evil things and worthy of such hopes
are those who make them and those who desire them and those who worship them.

And with evil labor he molds a vain god from the same clay,
he who a little while ago came into being out of earth
and in a little while goes back to that from which he was taken,
when the debt of the soul lent him is called in.

Yet his care is not that he must labor and die,
nor that his span of life is short;
rather he vies with goldsmiths and silversmiths
and copies the bronze-workers,
and holds it a glory to shape false things.

His heart is ashes, his hope cheaper than dirt,
and his life of less worth than clay,

He reckoned our life to be a plaything,
and existence a fair for making profit,
for one must make money, he says, from any source, even from evil.

For this one knows beyond all others that he is sinning,
when out of earthly stuff he makes brittle wares and graven images.

But most foolish of all, and more miserable than an infant’s soul,
are the enemies of your people who oppressed them.{b}

For they counted even every idol of the nations as gods,
which have no eyes to use for seeing,
no nostrils for drawing in air,
no ears for hearing,
no fingers on their hands for touching,
and feet that are idle for walking.

Moreover, they worship even the most hateful animals,
which, compared for stupidity, are worse than all others;

Nor do they even happen to be fair to look at, as animals go, so as to be wanted,
but they have fled both from God’s praise and from his blessing.{c}

notes.text: Or, with a slight change, “stirs desire in fools.”

verses.text:
So by creatures of that same sort they paid a fitting penalty,
tortured by swarms of vermin.

For on those tyrants a want that could not be avoided had to come,
but to these it had only to be shown how their foes were being tortured.

for a short time they were thrown into alarm for their correction,
having a token of rescue to bring the command of your law to mind.

For the one who turned was kept safe not by the thing he looked at,
but on account of you, who rescue all.

And in this too you persuaded our foes
that you are he who sets free from every harm.

but your sons not even the fangs of venom-spitting serpents overcame,
for your mercy came alongside and cured them.

For to call your sayings to mind they were stung,
and swiftly brought through safely,
so that they might not fall into deep forgetting
and be cut off from your good deeds.

For it was neither herb nor plaster that made them well,
but your word, Lord, which makes all things whole.

For you hold authority over life and over death,
and you bring down to the gates and bring up.

A man may kill through his evil,
but the spirit, once gone out, he does not bring back,
nor does he free the soul that has been taken.
To escape from your hand is impossible;

For the ungodly, who denied that they knew you,
were whipped by the might of your arm,
chased by strange rains and hailstorms and downpours that would not be begged off,
and eaten up by fire.{d}

For—the most amazing thing—in water, which puts out everything,
the fire burned even more strongly,
since the universe fights for the righteous.

For at one time the flame was tamed,
so as not to burn up the animals sent against the ungodly,
but that they themselves, on seeing it, might grasp
that God’s judgment was driving them;

and at another time, even in the midst of water, it blazed beyond fire’s own power,
to ruin the yield of an unrighteous land.

For your food{f} showed your kindness toward your children,
and, suiting the appetite of whoever ate it,
it turned into whatever each one desired.

Snow and ice{g} held out against fire and did not melt,
that they might know that it was fire that ruined the enemies’ harvests,
fire flaming in the hail
and lightning-flashing in the rains;

and this same fire, again, so that the righteous might be fed,
had forgotten even its own power.

For the creation that serves you, its maker,
is stretched tight to chastise the unrighteous,
and slackens to do good to those who rely on you.

So then too, being changed into everything,
it was in service to your gift that nourishes all,
according to the wish of those in want,

For what was not ruined by fire
melted simply when it was warmed by a brief sunbeam,

so that people would know they must get up before sunrise to thank you,
and must address you as daylight begins;

For the ungrateful man’s hope will thaw like winter’s hoarfrost
and run off like water that serves no purpose.

notes.text: The plague of hail and lightning (Exod 9:13–35).
The manna (Exod 16; Ps 78:25). Jewish tradition held that the manna tasted as each person wished.
“Snow and ice” here describe the manna (Num 11:7; Exod 16:14, 21).

verses.text:
Great are your judgments and hard to recount;
therefore souls without instruction went astray.

For when lawless men had supposed that they held a holy nation in their power,
they lay prisoners of darkness and captives of a long night,
shut in under their roofs,
exiles from the everlasting providence.{a}

For thinking to go unseen in their secret sins,
they were scattered under a dark curtain of forgetfulness,
horribly dismayed and thrown into panic by apparitions.

For not even the inner chamber that held them kept them free of fear,
but noises crashed around them and terrified them,
and gloomy phantoms with unsmiling faces appeared.

No force of fire had strength to give light,
nor did the bright flames of the stars endure to lighten that hateful night.

Only a self-kindled blaze showed through to them, full of fear,
and, terrified at the sight they could not see,
they thought the things they did see worse still.

The tricks of the magic art lay humbled,
and its boast of wisdom was put to a shameful test.

For those who promised to drive away terrors and disorders from a sick soul
were themselves sick with a fear that deserved laughter.

For even when nothing alarming was there to frighten them,
they were startled out of their wits by vermin creeping past and by reptiles hissing,

they perished trembling,
refusing even to look at the air, which can be fled from nowhere.

For wickedness is a cowardly thing, condemned by its own witness;{b}
squeezed by conscience, it always magnifies its troubles.
For fear is nothing but the surrender of the help that comes from reasoning;

and the weaker the expectation within,
the greater it reckons its ignorance of the cause that brings the torment.

But they, all through that night that was truly powerless,
that came upon them from the recesses of powerless Hades,
sleeping the same sleep,

And so whoever had dropped down there
was held fast, shut up in a prison without iron bars.

for they were all tied by a single chain of darkness.
Whether it was a whistling breeze,
a melodious song of birds in the thick branches,
or the rhythmic roar of rushing water,

or the harsh clatter of rocks tumbling down,
or the unseen racing of animals at play,
or the voice of wild beasts roaring in their utmost savagery,
or an echo rebounding from the mountains’ hollows,
it unstrung them with terror.

For the whole world was lit up with brilliant light
and went about its work unhindered,

notes.text: The ninth plague, darkness (Exod 10:21–23), is the subject of 17:1–18:4.
The Greek of the first line is difficult; Swete’s text repeats part of the second line.

verses.text:
and because they, though wronged before, were doing them no harm, they were thankful,
and begged their pardon for having been at odds with them.{b}

In place of these things you provided a pillar of flaming fire
as a guide for an unknown journey,
and a sun that would do no harm on their glorious wandering abroad.

For those others deserved to be robbed of light and imprisoned in darkness,
who had kept your sons shut up,
through whom the imperishable light of the law was to be given to the world.

After they decided to kill the babies of the holy ones,
when one child was abandoned and rescued,{c}
you removed their many children as punishment,
and drowned them all together in the mighty flood.

That night was made known beforehand to our fathers,{d}
so that, knowing surely the oaths in which they trusted, they might be of good courage.

By your people there was awaited
rescue for the righteous and ruin for the enemies;

for with that by which you took vengeance on our opponents,
with this you summoned us and gave us glory.

But the discordant cry of the enemies echoed back,
and a pitiful sound of mourning for children was carried abroad.

Slave and master were punished with like penalty,
and the commoner suffered the same as the king;

For though they had disbelieved everything because of their sorceries,
at the destruction of the firstborn they acknowledged the people to be God’s son.

For when quiet silence held all things in its embrace,
and night in her own swiftness was at midcourse,

your all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from the royal throne,
a stern warrior, into the midst of the doomed land,

Then at once apparitions in dreadful dreams troubled them,
and unexpected fears assailed them;

and one here, another there, flung down half dead,
made known the cause for which they were dying;

for the dreams that disturbed them had warned of this beforehand,
so that they might not perish without knowing why they suffered.

For a faultless man{h} hurried to defend them,
bringing the weapon of his own service,
prayer and the atoning offering of incense;
he stood against the fury and ended the calamity,
proving that he was your servant.

He overcame the anger{i} not by bodily strength,
not by the working of weapons,
but by a word he brought the chastiser under,
calling to mind the oaths and covenants of the fathers.

For when the dead were already piled in heaps on each other,
he took his stand between and restrained the fury,
and blocked its path to the living.

To these the destroyer yielded; these he{k} feared;
for only to taste of the wrath was enough.

notes.text: The sense of the second line is uncertain; it may mean “and asked as a favor that they would depart.”
Moses (Exod 2:1–10). The “mighty water” is the Red Sea (Exod 14).
Or “the fathers already leading the songs of praise.”
Greek ochlon, “the multitude,” probably a slip for cholon, “the wrath,” as many editors read.
Exod 28. Philo and Josephus interpret the high priest’s vestments as an image of the cosmos.

verses.text:
But upon the ungodly a merciless anger pressed to the end,
for he knew beforehand even what they would do:

how, though they themselves had permitted your people to depart
and hurriedly sent them on their way,
they would change their minds and pursue them.

For with their mourning still in their hands,
and while they were wailing over the tombs of the dead,
they drew upon themselves another senseless thought,
and those whom they had entreated to leave and thrown out,
these they hunted as runaways.

For the necessity they had earned dragged them to this end,
and cast into them oblivion of what had befallen,
so that they might fill up beforehand the chastisement still lacking to their torments,

and that your people might experience an incredible journey,
while they themselves met a strange death.

There was beheld the cloud that shaded the encampment,
the rising of dry land out of water that had stood there before,
out of the Red Sea a road with nothing in its way,
and a green-bearing plain out of the violent surge,

through which the whole nation passed, protected by your hand,
after gazing on marvelous wonders.

For they ranged like horses,
and leaped like lambs,
praising you, Lord, who delivered them.

For they still recalled what happened during their stay,
how in place of livestock the land produced gnats,
and in place of fish the river belched out a swarm of frogs.

Later on they saw also a new brood of birds,
when, carried away by desire, they asked for dainty dishes;
for, to satisfy them, quails came up from the sea.{b}

Others{d} had refused to receive strangers when they arrived,
but these made slaves of guests who were their benefactors.

And not only so, but there will be some punishment for those others,
because they received foreigners with hostility;

but these, after receiving them with festal celebrations,
afflicted with dreadful labors those who had already shared the same rights.

And they were struck with blindness too,
as those others were at the doors of the righteous one,{e}{f}
when, wrapped in gaping darkness,
each went seeking the passage through his own doors.

For things of dry land were turned into water creatures,
and swimming things went over onto the earth;{h}

Fire retained its strength in water,
and water forgot its fire-quenching nature.

For in all respects, Lord, you have made your people great and glorified them,
and you did not overlook them, standing by them at every time and place.

notes.text: The thought recalls a new creation; compare 19:18–21.
Swete’s text, following Vaticanus, places the clause “for they practiced a more bitter hatred of strangers” at the end of verse 13; the numbering of verses 13–14 differs among editions.
The Greek text of this verse is uncertain in places; Swete marks two words as doubtful.
The Israelites with their cattle passed through the sea; the frogs came up onto land.
